transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-12-15
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: 1h12m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (Redwood SRE), Maya (Product), Samir (NovaCore Head ML), Olivia (Infra), Lee (ML perf), Jasmine (Security)

Summary: Deep technical discussion comparing kernel selection and runtime behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on GPUs, exploration of CUDA graphs for steady-state throughput, KV cache behavior across long-context workloads, batching strategies and quantization tradeoffs, and implications for running in VPC/on-prem environments. Team agreed to run a short POC with NovaCore workload and exchange profiler traces.

Topics covered: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM quantization paths, vLLM continuous batching, CUDA graphs warmup vs dynamic tracing, KV cache eviction and cold-start latencies, network egress in VPC, orchestration considerations for Dedicated vs Private deployment.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Quick intros? We have a bunch of folks from NovaCore, want to make sure we tailor the deep dive to the SKUs you run and the workloads you care about.
[00:14] Samir: Yeah thanks Alex. Samir here. We're evaluating options to reduce per-token cost on long context ranking tasks, and latency matters for some synchronous use cases. We run a mix of 8k and 32k contexts, mostly on A100 and one cluster of H100s.
[00:30] Priya: Great. Priya from Redwood. We'll focus on profiling and explain where kernel selection differences show up between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM. Also we'll demo CUDA graph traces for steady-state throughput.
[00:44] Olivia: Quick question — we have VPC peering to our infra and strict egress controls. Any special notes for Private / on-prem?
[00:52] Daniel: From the runtime side, Private deployment needs KMS hooks and audit logs, but perf is essentially the same; network impacts only when KV cache or model weights are fetched remotely.
[01:06] Lee: Can you define what you mean by kernel selection? Sometimes our measurements show odd spikes mid-sequence.
[01:14] Priya: Sure — kernel selection here means the inference engine choosing specific CUDA kernels based on layer type, dtype, sequence length, and packing. Example: for attention, TensorRT-LLM may pick an optimized fused multihead-attn kernel for FP16 with head_dim multiples, whereas vLLM's runtime (using cuBLAS/cuDNN or custom kernels) might choose a different path and do more splitting which changes occupancy. That leads to throughput and latency differences, especially at short sequences or odd token lengths.
[01:45] Samir: Are we seeing up to 20-30% diff in tokens/sec between them in your benchmarks?
[01:52] Priya: In certain shapes, yes. For large batch steady-state workloads TensorRT-LLM with TensorRT kernels and aggressive kernel fusion often wins, particularly when using INT8/quantized paths and when cuBLAS LT kernels are available. But vLLM can beat it at dynamic batching for low-latency single-request tail since it maintains a careful KV cache and continuous batching pipeline.
[02:18] Alex: We prepared an example microbenchmark with 8k context and variable prompt lengths. Priya, do you want to talk through the NVTX traces?
[02:26] Priya: Sure — I uploaded a screenshot to the call. On the NVTX timeline you can see the CUDA Graph capture window: when we capture a graph after a warmup of 8 iterations, the seq2seq steady-state becomes a single CUDA Graph with pre-linked kernels which removes launch overhead. That reduces per-token latency by about 8-12% in our runs. However, the caveat is dynamic shapes — graphs are shape-specific, so you either capture many graph variants or re-capture on change, which has capture overhead.
[03:05] Lee: So for NovaCore where prompts vary heavily, capturing all shapes isn't practical. Does Redwood do any automatic graph invalidation/recapture?
[03:14] Priya: We recommend a hybrid: capture for the highest-volume token shapes and fallback to JIT paths for rare shapes. Redwood's runtime can maintain a graph cache keyed by (model_version, dtype, seq_len_bucket). We typically bucket sequence lengths — e.g., 1-64, 65-512, 513-2048 — to limit graph explosion.
[03:40] Samir: About KV cache — our long-context ranking uses caching aggressively. We're seeing cold-start spikes when first key is requested after a deploy. Any suggestions?
[03:51] Daniel: Cold-start is usually due to allocator fragmentation and weight paging. For KV cache specifically, warmup priming requests that populate the KV store are cheap, but if your model version rotates frequently the cache is invalidated. For Dedicated instances we support pinned model weights and persistent KV cache for a session which helps.
[04:12] Olivia: Is persistent KV cache compatible with quantized INT8 kernels? We worry about numeric drift.
[04:20] Priya: Good point. INT8 quantization is sensitive. TensorRT-LLM's INT8 kernels assume calibration and can have different output distributions; persistent KV cache stores raw key/value tensors so numerics match inference path. The risk is mixing quantized and non-quantized paths for the same model state; don't do mixing across clients without explicit conversion. We advise pinning quantization config per model version.
[04:48] Samir: Can you talk numbers — latency and throughput differences you typically see between TR-LLM and vLLM for long-context 32k workloads?
[04:56] Priya: Ballpark: on H100, with FP16 and good kernel support, TensorRT-LLM can get ~12-18 tokens/sec for 32k-ish sequences in batch-4 steady-state; vLLM with continuous KV and smaller kernel fusions may do 8-14 tokens/sec but with lower single-request tail at batch-1 due to better async batching. Those numbers vary a lot based on head_dim multiples, layernorm ops fusion, and quantization. We'll share detailed traces.
[05:28] Lee: We saw one run where cudaGraphs gave worse perf because of increased memory working set. Why would that happen?
[05:36] Priya: That happens when graph capture holds temporary buffers across invocations and prevents reuse, or if the graph includes debug counters; also if you capture with large batch but then run with smaller batch the allocator may reserve more. There is an allocator tuning tradeoff.
[05:52] Alex: Quick interjection — there's also kernel selection when using TF32 vs FP16 vs INT8. Sometimes switching dtype changes which kernel path is taken and changes perf dramatically.
[06:02] Samir: On the topic of batching — we need to balance latency vs throughput. Our user surface is mixed: most are async but some are synchronous with 150-300ms SLO. Any guidance?
[06:10] Priya: For mixed workloads, configure two endpoint tiers: low-latency (single-request optimized) and throughput (batched). Redwood routing can route short requests to low-latency pool with smaller batch windows and no CUDA Graph capture to avoid shape stalls. For throughput endpoints, use larger batch windows and capture graphs for the dominant shapes.
[06:34] Jasmine: Security question — when running in our VPC, can Redwood still collect NVTX/CUDA traces? We're not comfortable with traces leaving our network.
[06:44] Daniel: For Private deployments, traces can be collected to a local S3-equivalent and only redacted artifacts can be sent to Redwood. We have a policy for PII scrubbing and only accept aggregated perf metrics for support. For Dedicated hosted clusters we can also require encrypted transit and customer-managed keys.
[07:06] Priya: Back to kernel selection: a practical debugging step is to run a per-layer flame graph comparing time spent in attention, MLP, and add/softmax kernels across the two runtimes. Often a single layer with non-power-of-two head dims causes the big difference.
[07:28] Lee: We have a 4096 head dim problem. Any tips for alignment?
[07:33] Priya: If head_dim % 32 != 0 you may lose fused kernel options; padding heads or using partitioned attention kernels can help. TensorRT may provide an alternate kernel if the architecture supports it. vLLM more often splits into smaller GEMM ops which can be less efficient.
[07:50] Samir: Quantization — we want to try 4-bit for cost. What's the risk?
[07:56] Priya: 4-bit quant reduces memory and can increase throughput, but models need proper quantization-aware calibration. For some generation tasks, 4-bit causes quality regressions; we use mixed-precision mixes: quantize MatMuls but keep layernorm and softmax in higher precision. Also per-channel scales and outlier handling matter. TensorRT-LLM's quant kernels are highly optimized but assume calibration artifacts. vLLM supports quantization via QLinear-like paths and can integrate with bitsandbytes.
[08:26] Olivia: Do you have recommendations for our on-prem H100 cluster sizing? We currently use 8xH100 per node.
[08:33] Daniel: For 32k contexts, per-request memory is large — you want the largest GPU memory available; H100 with 80GB or 160GB variants reduce cross-GPU sharding complexity. If you shard across NVLink nodes, ensure PCIe/NVLink topology is accounted for in kernel placement. We often recommend 80GB minimum per GPU for 32k long-context with 7B-ish models; for 70B+ you will need model parallelism.
[08:57] Priya: Also watch for PCIe host bandwidth; large KV cache read/writes can bottleneck if using CPU staging. Keep KV cache on device when possible.
[09:10] Lee: Any tips for measuring tail latency?
[09:13] Priya: Use p99 and p999 histograms, instrument end-to-end including network hop in VPC, and capture NVTX for kernels that correspond to tail spikes. Also correlate with GC in host agent, allocator stalls, and CUDA stream sync points.
[09:33] Samir: How does Redwood handle model rollouts without flushing KV cache?
[09:38] Alex: We support canary rollouts with versioned endpoints. If you need sticky sessions we can pin client sessions to instances so KV remains valid. For rolling updates we recommend staggered draining and priming new instances.
[09:55] Priya: Let's look at the example traces. On this screen you can see vLLM's continuous batching queue with variable op latencies, and TensorRT's batched path that is flatter but with higher single-launch overhead. At [example timestamp] you can see a big spike when a non-captured shape hits the TRT path — that's a recapture.
[10:20] Olivia: Is it safe to auto-capture graphs in Prod? We worry about capture storms.
[10:28] Priya: You should rate-limit captures and use a sampling policy: e.g., only capture when shape frequency > X per minute, and limit to N captures per GPU per hour. Also capture during low-traffic windows if possible.
[10:44] Samir: Bench question — what perf delta do you see when enabling cuBLAS LT (tensor cores) vs standard cuBLAS?
[10:51] Priya: cuBLAS LT can give 1.2x-2x improvements for certain matmul shapes on Hopper when the kernels match. But it requires appropriate alignment and datatypes; fallback is to standard cuBLAS which is sometimes slower. Runtime will choose LT when it finds a supported config.
[11:07] Lee: Any gotchas for multi-GPU models using tensor-parallel kernels?
[11:11] Daniel: Sync points and NVLink bandwidth. Kernel selection also changes: some fused kernels that work on single-GPU have multi-GPU equivalents with extra comms, which can increase latency. Monitor NCCL saturation and prefer larger micro-batching inside all-reduce where possible.
[11:27] Priya: Also watch for kernel auto-tuning phases during the first few minutes after deploy. Those can skew short-term perf numbers. We usually run a warmup job for 10-20 minutes before measuring.
[11:40] Samir: Can Redwood run these warmups automatically?
[11:43] Alex: Yes, we have a warmup job that can replay typical prompts to prime weights, caches, and kernel caches. We'll share the warmup script.
[11:52] [12:00] Priya: Slight transcription hiccup — the NVTX callout shows a memory copy that looked like a 600ms stall but actually was multiple small copies aggregated by the tracer. So sometimes profiler aggregation can overstate single-copy cost.
[12:12] Lee: About memory — is there a recommended allocator? We use default CUDA malloc.
[12:17] Daniel: Use a pooled allocator with best-fit and reuse semantics (we use jemalloc on host and custom device pooling). It reduces fragmentation and cold-start overhead. Ensure the allocator can release to the OS if you're running multi-tenant.
[12:33] Samir: For our POC, we want to test three setups: (1) TensorRT-LLM with FP16 + CUDA Graphs, (2) vLLM continuous batching FP16, (3) TensorRT-LLM with 4-bit quant on selected matmuls. Is that feasible in a week?
[12:47] Priya: Yes — provided you share the prompt families and token histograms. We'll run side-by-side with identical harness and sampling for p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[12:56] Alex: We'll also instrument with NVTX and export cudagraph traces for the TR runs.
[13:02] Olivia: For on-prem, do you need root access to install tracing libs?
[13:07] Daniel: We need an agent installed with appropriate privileges; for air-gapped environments we can provide an offline agent bundle. We won't ship any data out without your approval.
[13:17] Jasmine: Security — if we send traces to Redwood, can we obfuscate prompt text?
[13:21] Priya: Yes — we recommend redacting or hashing prompt text before upload. Our support tools accept hashed or token-only traces.
[13:30] Samir: One more nit — what about scheduler jitter from Kubernetes when pods get scheduled?
[13:35] Daniel: For Dedicated/Private we recommend node-pinning and GPU isolation. Avoid preemption and use Guaranteed QoS. Also set CPU/memory reservations for the inference agent to avoid OOM kills.
[13:51] Priya: Let's call out a few concrete metrics to capture during the POC: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, tensor/core utilization, NVLink/PCIe counters, allocator fragmentation, and capture frequency for CUDA Graphs.
[14:07] Lee: We'll provide token length histogram and the set of 20 high-frequency prompts.
[14:12] Alex: Great. To wrap, I'll read the next steps. We'll share the microbenchmark script and config, Redwood will run three candidate setups, NovaCore will provide workloads and infra details, and we'll reconvene with traces.
[14:28] Samir: Sounds good. Quick question on pricing: if we choose Dedicated with pinned weights and persistent KV cache, is there an extra cost?
[14:35] Alex: Yes, Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing and some features like persistent cache and extended retention are add-ons. We'll send a pricing note after the call.
[14:44] Priya: Final note — for production, we recommend starting with a small dedicated pool for the throughput path and a hosted low-latency pool for burst/sync, then move more traffic as perf and cost stabilize.
[14:58] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts.
